lesson.title: What this chapter is trying to do
lesson.lead: Sourabh sir's framing: every supervised model has parameters, and learning means finding the best ones.

blocks.text: A regression or neural-network model has parameters, for example a and b in y = ax + b. 'Learning' means finding the parameter values that fit the data best. To say 'best' you need a score for how wrong the model is: the loss. The best parameters sit at the bottom of the loss. Lecture 9 is about how to walk down to that bottom when you cannot solve for it by hand.

Topic

blocks.label: Weightage
blocks.text: MFML's comprehensive exam (open book, 6 Dec) is mostly after the mid-sem: Sourabh sir said lectures 9 onwards carry about 70-75% and lectures 1-8 about 25-30%. Gradient-descent numericals are in every end-sem paper I read: Feb 2026 Q4 (8 marks), Mar 2026 Q3 (7) and Q4 (4), 2024 Q4 (7). So this block is roughly 8 to 11 marks, from a few question types.

lesson.title: Topic 1: Why optimise? The loss (slides 1-4)
lesson.lead: Turn 'find the best line' into 'find the lowest point of a score'.

blocks.text: Slide 3 gives data: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3.1, 4.9, 7.3, 9.1, with the model ŷ = ax + b (ŷ is the predicted y, a the slope, b the intercept).
L(a, b) = Σ (y − ŷ)² = Σ (y − (a·x + b))²
blocks.caption: slide 4: each term is a squared gap, so positive and negative gaps do not cancel

blocks.text: The second line hugs the points, and its loss is far smaller. All of ML training is this: try parameters, and prefer the ones with the smaller loss. Finding a and b that make L smallest is an optimisation problem.

blocks.label: Add-on from Sourabh sir's companion
blocks.text: The companion (Lecture 9) works the same two guesses. The exam writes the loss with a half in front and the error as ŷ − y: J = ½ Σ (ŷ − y)². Squaring makes the order irrelevant, and the ½ only cancels the 2 when you differentiate.

lesson.title: Topic 2: Zero gradient and the second-derivative test (slides 5-7)
lesson.lead: At the bottom of a valley the ground is flat. For easy functions you can solve for that spot.

blocks.text: Slide 5: we move along the negative gradient until the gradient is zero. That point is a valley, a local minimum. Zero gradient only says 'flat', so slide 7 adds the second-derivative test: positive means a minimum, negative means a maximum.

l(x) = x⁴ + 7x³ + 5x² − 17x + 3
dl/dx = 4x³ + 21x² + 10x − 17        second derivative = 12x² + 42x + 10
blocks.caption: slide 7

blocks.text: The deepest valley (global minimum) is x = −4.48. This worked because a cubic is easy to solve. Real loss functions cannot be solved by hand, so slide 8 says we follow the negative gradient instead.

blocks.label: How to spot it
blocks.text: 'Find the critical points and classify them': set the gradient to zero, then use the second derivative (or the Hessian in two variables, Lecture 8).

lesson.title: Topic 3: The gradient descent rule (slides 8-10)
lesson.lead: Walk downhill: feel the tilt, step against it, repeat.

blocks.text: The picture
You are blindfolded on a hill. You feel which way the ground tilts under your feet, take a small step downhill, and feel again. You stop when the ground is flat.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: The low part of the loss: the minimum. Where the parameters are best.
The value of the function, for example f(x) = 4.
How fast the height changes as you move, and in which direction. Positive tilt: the ground rises to the right, so downhill is left. Negative: downhill is right. Zero: flat.
A big gradient number: the height changes quickly. Gentle means a small number.
How far you move for each unit of tilt (called the learning rate elsewhere).

blocks.text: The rule (slide 9)
wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η∇f(wₜ)
blocks.caption: Slide 9 writes x(i+1) = x(i) − γᵢ((∇f)(x(i)))ᵀ: its γ is our η and its x is our w. Step against the gradient; for small enough η, f(wₜ₊₁) ≤ f(wₜ).

items: The slides write the gradient ∇f as a row of slopes and the point as a column, so they add ᵀ to turn the row into a column. The numbers are the same either way: take each partial derivative, scale it by η, subtract it from the matching coordinate.
Steep ground gives a big step. As the ground flattens near the bottom, the step shrinks by itself.

blocks.text: What the step size does
Take f(x) = (x − 3)², minimum at 3, gradient 2(x − 3), start at 0. Each step multiplies the gap to 3 by (1 − 2η).

head: η
x: 0 → ?
What happens
rows: each jump is bigger: blows up

blocks.text: Too small is slow; too large overshoots or diverges (slide 11). That is why decay, bold driver and line search exist: they are ways of choosing η.
Slide 10 example, worked by hand

f(x) = ½ xᵀAx + bᵀx with A = [[2, 1], [1, 20]], b = (−5, −3), start (−3, −1). The slide gives no step size (it runs MATLAB code), so I use η = 0.05 for the demonstration. The column form of the slide's gradient is A·x + b.

Step 1 by hand: A·x0 = (2(−3) + 1(−1), 1(−3) + 20(−1)) = (−7, −23); gradient = (−7, −23) + (−5, −3) = (−12, −26); x1 = (−3, −1) − 0.05·(−12, −26) = (−2.4, 0.3). f decreases every step. The true minimum is (2.487, 0.026). The y-gradient is 20 times steeper than the x-gradient: this mismatch is why plain GD zig-zags, and the reason for momentum in Lecture 11.

blocks.label: Slide 10's step size
blocks.text: The slide does not state η. The 0.05 and the table are my illustration, not the slide's numbers.

blocks.text: The approach

items: Write f and find the gradient: one partial derivative per variable.
Note η (work out ηₜ first if a schedule is given).
Put the current point into the gradient.
Subtract: new = old − η × gradient, coordinate by coordinate.
Repeat for each iteration and show every line.
Check: f should decrease.

blocks.label: Marks
blocks.text: Show the gradient formula, the gradient value at each point, η, and the update. The commonest slip is dropping a term when differentiating.

lesson.title: How do I decide η in a problem?
lesson.lead: Usually you do not decide it. Read the verb in the question.

head: The question says
What to do
Where
rows: Hessian, eigenvalues, then 0 < η < 2/λmax (all four mean the same)
Minimise φ(η) = f(x − η·gradient) over η
one step is given, 'find the learning rate'
Read the update backwards: η = (old − new) / gradient
Start small; if f rises, halve it (slide 12)

blocks.label: At exactly 2/λmax
blocks.text: The error bounces with the same size forever, so 'largest stable' is 'just below 2/λmax'.

lesson.title: Important: the stable step size (add-on)
lesson.lead: Not on the slides. It is in Sourabh sir's Lecture 10 companion and Problems 26 and 27.

blocks.text: GD on a quadratic converges for 0 < η < 2 / λmax(H)
blocks.caption: λmax = the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian H

blocks.text: Carry this line on your formula sheet. Cues in a question: 'stable', 'converges', 'oscillates', 'explodes', 'largest learning rate'.
Sample calculation (Problem 26's function)
f(x, y) = x² + y² + xy − 3x. First derivatives: 2x + y − 3 and 2y + x. Differentiate again for the Hessian (Lecture 8, slide 16), then take its eigenvalues.

H = [ 2  1 ]
    [ 1  2 ]
det(H − λI) = (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0  →  λ = 1 or 3
stable for 0 < η < 2/3
blocks.caption: check: 1 + 3 = trace 4 and 1 × 3 = determinant 3

blocks.text: What you write in the exam: the Hessian, its eigenvalues, and the line 'stable for 0 < η < 2/λmax = 2/3'. Nothing more.
Where 2/λ comes from (to understand it, not to write)

On a bowl of steepness λ, one step multiplies the gap to the minimum by (1 − ηλ). The gap shrinks only if that multiplier lies between −1 and 1, which means 0 < ηλ < 2, so 0 < η < 2/λ. With two directions the step must suit both, so the steepest direction (λmax) sets the limit.

lesson.title: Step-size behaviour: monotone, oscillating, divergent (background and recipe)
lesson.lead: How to work out, for any new function, whether gradient descent crawls in, zigzags in, or blows up, and which η is safe. Saurabh sir writes α for the step size; here it is η.

blocks.text: Idea 1 · Measure the distance to the answer
Let x* be the minimum. What matters is the **error e = x − x***. If e shrinks to 0, gradient descent **converges**.
Idea 2 · On a bowl, one step multiplies the error by a fixed number
Take any parabola f(x) = a(x − c)² + k, whose minimum is at c.

groups.label: Derivation
groups.note: Every step multiplies the error by the same number r. After t steps, e_{t} = rᵗ · e₀.

blocks.text: Idea 3 · What multiplying by r again and again does

blocks.label: Read r in two looks
blocks.text: The **sign** of r says whether x flips side each step. The **size** of r (|r| < 1 or not) says whether the error shrinks or grows.
Idea 4 · Turn the r ranges into η ranges

**Picture:** η is a jump size. A small jump stops before the bottom; the perfect jump lands on it; a medium jump goes past but lands closer; a huge jump lands higher up the other side than where it started.
Try it: set the curvature c (= f″) and drag η. The presets show each case.
More than one variable

items: If f splits into separate squares (f = 3x² + 5y²), each coordinate has its own r: r_{x} = 1 − 6η, r_{y} = 1 − 10η.

All coordinates must converge, so the **steepest direction (largest f″) sets the limit: η < 2/f″_{max}**. That is why [Sourabh P33](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch11/f-adaptive/8) diverges in w₂ (f″ = 20) while w₁ (f″ = 2) is fine.
With cross terms (like 2xy), use the **eigenvalues of the Hessian** in place of f″: η < 2/λmax (the board above, and [Optimizers Set Q5](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch11/f-adaptive/28)).

blocks.text: The recipe for any new problem

head: Question type
Steps
rows: 1. f″ for each variable (or Hessian eigenvalues). 2. r = 1 − ηf″ for each. 3. Read r off the Idea 3 table. 4. Verdict = the worst one: any |r| > 1 ⇒ diverges.
B · "Here is a run of numbers: find η and classify"

1. Subtract x* to get errors. 2. Divide each error by the previous ⇒ r; it must be the **same** every time (if not, it is not plain GD: try momentum, [Sourabh Optimizers Set Q7](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch11/f-momentum/22)(b)). 3. η = (1 − r)/f″. 4. Classify from r.
C · "For which η does it converge?"
1. f″_{max} (or λmax). 2. 0 < η < 2/f″_{max}; monotone below 1/f″_{max}, oscillating between 1/f″_{max} and 2/f″_{max}.
D · "Which η reaches the minimum in one step?"

blocks.label: What to write in the exam
blocks.text:
GD on f gives e_{t+1} = (1 − ηf″)e_{t} with f″ = __, so r = __.
Since __ < r < __, the iterates [converge monotonically / oscillate but converge / diverge].
Convergence needs |1 − ηf″| < 1 ⇔ 0 < η < 2/f″ = __.
Then check one step by hand (x₁ = x₀ − ηf′(x₀)).

Practise: [the worked example](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch09/f-gd/5) (a new function, all four types), then [Sourabh Optimizers Set Q7](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch11/f-momentum/22) (Type B from data) and [Sourabh P33](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch11/f-adaptive/8) (two variables).

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: **On a bowl, every GD step multiplies the distance to the bottom by r = 1 − η·f″.** Read the sign of r for flipping and its size for shrinking.

worked.title: GD · Practice (type a): f = w1² + w2² from (4, 2)

problem.text: My own practice question, built on the function Sourabh sir uses in class.
Consider f(w1, w2) = w1² + w2². Using gradient descent with step size η = 0.1 and starting point (w1, w2) = (4, 2), compute the point after two iterations.

steps.label: Formula (slide 9)
steps.text: wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η∇f(wₜ). Apply it to each coordinate.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: f decreases: 20, 12.8, 8.192. Each step multiplies both coordinates by 0.8, so after n steps you are at (4, 2) × 0.8ⁿ; for n = 2 that is (2.56, 1.28).

steps.label: Step-size lesson
steps.text: With η = 0.5 the first step is (4 − 4, 2 − 2) = (0, 0): the minimum in one step. That best η is what line search finds.

worked.answer: After two iterations the point is (2.56, 1.28), with f = 8.192.

worked.title: GD · Sourabh sir Problem 26: one step, two learning rates

problem.text: Minimise f(x, y) = x² + y² + xy − 3x by gradient descent from (0, 0). (a) Write the update equations for x and y. (b) Do one step with η = 0.1 and, separately, one step with η = 1. (c) Compute f at the start and after each step. (d) Find the true minimiser and the largest stable learning rate.

steps.label: Formulas
steps.text: Slide 9: wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η∇f(wₜ). Hessian: slide 16 of Lecture 8. Eigenvalues: det(H − λI) = 0. Stable step: 0 < η < 2/λmax (add-on).

steps.label: (a) Update equations
steps.text: ∂f/∂x = 2x + y − 3 and ∂f/∂y = 2y + x. So x(new) = x − η(2x + y − 3) and y(new) = y − η(2y + x).

steps.label: (c) f at each point
steps.text: f(0, 0) = 0. f(0.3, 0) = 0.09 − 0.9 = **−0.81**. f(3, 0) = 9 − 9 = **0**. The big step went far but ended at the same height: it overshot. Judge a step by f, not by distance.

steps.label: (d) Minimiser
steps.text: Set the gradient to zero: 2x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 0. Then x = −2y, so −4y + y = 3, y = −1, x = 2. **Minimiser (2, −1), f = −3.**

steps.label: (d) Hessian and eigenvalues
steps.text: fxx = 2, fxy = 1, fyy = 2, so H = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. det(H − λI) = (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0, so λ = 1 or 3. Check: sum 4 = trace, product 3 = determinant.

steps.label: (d) Stable step
steps.text: **0 < η < 2/λmax = 2/3.** So η = 0.1 is fine and η = 1 is too big, which is why it overshot.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text: Dropping the −3 in ∂f/∂x; judging a step only by how far it moved.

worked.title: GD · Feb 2026 end-sem Q4: regression loss, Hessian, decay schedule (8 marks)

problem.text: A retail shop wants to predict their sales corresponding to the money they spent on advertisement using the following data. A linear regression model with bias is assumed: ŷi = w0 + w1·xi. [8 marks]

head: Money spent for advertisement in ten thousands (x)
Sales in lacs (y)

problem.text: The model parameters are learned by minimizing the Squared Error loss function J(w0, w1) = ½ Σ (ŷi − yi)², sum over i = 1 to 2, using gradient descent.

(a) Formulate the Squared Error loss function J(w0, w1) explicitly for the given dataset. Compute the Hessian matrix of J with respect to w0 and w1, and use it to prove that J is a convex function of the parameters (w0, w1). [3M]
(b) Compute the gradient of the Squared Error loss function: ∇J. [1M]

(c) Taking the initial parameter values w0 = 0, w1 = 0, perform two iterations of gradient descent using the inverse decaying learning rate schedule with initial learning rate η0 = 0.1, k = 0.4, where t = 1, 2, .. denote the iteration index. Show the updated parameter values after each iteration. [4M]

steps.label: Symbols
steps.text: Slide letters: loss L(a, b) on slide 4 (b is the intercept, a the slope), so w0 is b and w1 is a. The decayed rate is ηₜ (slide 16); the exam calls it η. In the Hessian slide (Lecture 8, slide 16) the variables are x, y, so here x is w0 and y is w1.

steps.label: Formulas
steps.text: Slide 15: wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − ηₜ∇J. Slide 16: inverse decay ηₜ = {{ η₀ // 1 + k·t }}. Lecture 8 slides 16-17: Hessian [[fxx, fxy], [fxy, fyy]]; Sylvester's criterion: fxx > 0 and fxx·fyy − fxy² > 0 means positive definite. 'Positive definite means convex' is the exam key's reason and is an add-on.

steps.label: (a) Build J
steps.text: ŷ = w0 + w1·x. J = ½ [(w0 + 5w1 − 3)² + (w0 + 6w1 − 5)²]. The slide writes the gap as y − ŷ; squaring makes the order irrelevant.

steps.label: (a) Sylvester
steps.text: fxx = 2 > 0. fxx·fyy − fxy² = 2 × 61 − 11² = 122 − 121 = 1 > 0. So H is positive definite and **J is convex**.

steps.label: Why step 2 jumps back
steps.text: Step 1 overshot (w1 went far past the valley bottom), so the gradient at the new point is large and positive, and step 2 pulls back. The decay only shrinks ηₜ from 0.0714 to 0.0556. That is normal here, not an error.

steps.label: Rounding
steps.text: Keeping η₁, η₂ as fractions gives (−1.0119, −5.5278). Both are acceptable.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text: Forgetting to prove convexity; computing ηₜ after the update instead of before; using the old gradient in iteration 2.

worked.title: GD · 2024 end-sem Q4: the plain-GD part (momentum part to come)

problem.text: Consider the function of two variables f(x, y) = (x − 1)² + (y − 1)². Suppose you apply gradient descent algorithm with momentum with initial values x0 = 1.5, y0 = 1.5, the learning parameter α = 0.05 and the momentum parameter β = 0.8 to find the point at which f(x, y) attains its global minimum. Find (x1, y1), (x2, y2) using first two iterations of gradient descent algorithm with momentum. Also find (a1, b1), (a2, b2) using first two iterations of gradient descent algorithm using the same initial values x0 = 1.5, y0 = 1.5 and the learning parameter α = 0.05. Conclude whether there is any advantage of using the gradient descent algorithm with momentum instead of just using the gradient descent algorithm? [7 marks]

problem.label: Status
problem.text: This entry does only the plain-GD half, (a1, b1) and (a2, b2). The momentum half and the comparison come with Lecture 11.

steps.label: Formula (slide 9)
steps.text: Notation: this paper's symbol is kept, **α = 0.05 is the step size** (η on the lecture boards). Plain GD: xₜ₊₁ = xₜ − α∇f(xₜ), applied to each coordinate.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The minimum is (1, 1). The gap shrinks by a factor 0.9 each step (0.5, 0.45, 0.405). Keep these two points for the comparison with momentum.

worked.title: GD · Step-size behaviour: classify three learning rates on 4(x − 2)² + 1

problem.text: f(x) = 4(x − 2)² + 1, start x₀ = 3. (a) Classify gradient descent for η = 0.05, 0.2 and 0.3, and give x₁, x₂ for each. (b) Give the range of η for which GD converges, and where it is monotone or oscillating. (c) Which η reaches the minimum in one step?

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The step-size recipe: r = 1 − ηf″ decides monotone, oscillating or divergent; the cut-offs are 1/f″ and 2/f″.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text:
1. f′, f″ and the minimum x*.
2. Multiplier r = 1 − ηf″.
3. (a) r for each η, classify, and write the first iterates.
4. (b) 0 < η < 2/f″, split at 1/f″.
5. (c) η = 1/f″.
6. Check one step by hand.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: η = step size (Saurabh sir writes α). e = x − x* = error. r = the number each step multiplies e by.

steps.label: STEP 2 · The multiplier
steps.text:
e_new = (1 − ηf″) · e = **(1 − 8η) · e**
Start error e₀ = x₀ − x* = 3 − 2 = 1

steps.label: STEP 4 · (a) η = 0.2
steps.text:
r = 1 − 8 × 0.2 = 1 − 1.6 = **−0.6**
−1 < r < 0 ⇒ **oscillating convergence**
Errors: 1, −0.6, 0.36 ⇒ x = 3, **1.4**, **2.36** (jumps over 2, lands closer)

steps.label: STEP 6 · (b) Safe range
steps.text:
Need |1 − 8η| < 1 ⇒ −1 < 1 − 8η < 1
Right half: η > 0
Left half: 8η < 2 ⇒ η < 2/8 = **0.25**
Converges for **0 < η < 0.25**: monotone for η < 1/8 = 0.125, oscillating for 0.125 < η < 0.25.

steps.label: STEP 8 · Check one step by hand
Answers at a glance
steps.text: (a) η = 0.05: r = 0.6, monotone (2.6, 2.36). η = 0.2: r = −0.6, oscillating (1.4, 2.36). η = 0.3: r = −1.4, diverges (0.6, 3.96). (b) 0 < η < 0.25; monotone below 0.125, oscillating above. (c) η = 0.125.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Using f′ instead of f″ for the curvature.
• Forgetting to measure from x* = 2 (the error, not x).
• Saying "diverges" for −1 < r < 0: it zigzags but converges.
• Reading η off r directly instead of η = (1 − r)/f″.

worked.answer: r = 1 − 8η: η = 0.05 monotone, 0.2 oscillating, 0.3 diverges; converges for 0 < η < 0.25; one step at η = 0.125.
worked.priorityWhy: Step-size behaviour: the recipe for every 'which α' question

flashcards.back: wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η∇f(wₜ). Step against the gradient; the ᵀ turns the slide's row gradient into a column.

flashcards.front: Why do we subtract the gradient?
flashcards.back: The gradient points uphill (direction of steepest increase). We want the minimum, so we step the opposite way.

flashcards.front: What does the step size η do, and what goes wrong if it is too small or too large? (slide 11)
flashcards.back: It scales each step. Too small: very slow. Too large: overshoots, may fail to converge or diverge.
wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − ηₜ∇J, where ηₜ gets smaller with time.
Exponential: ηₜ = η₀·e^(−kt). Inverse: ηₜ = η₀ / (1 + k·t). k controls the rate of decay.

flashcards.front: Gradient is zero. How do you tell minimum from maximum? (slide 7)
flashcards.back: Second derivative: positive means a local minimum, negative means a local maximum.

flashcards.front: Hessian test for a minimum in two variables (Lecture 8, slides 16-17)
flashcards.back: fxx > 0 and fxx·fyy − fxy² > 0 (Sylvester): the Hessian is positive definite, so a minimum. For convexity the exam key uses the same test.

flashcards.front: Stable step size on a quadratic (add-on)
flashcards.back: 0 < η < 2/λmax(H), the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian.

flashcards.front: 'Perform k iterations of gradient descent': the steps
flashcards.back: Slope, scale, subtract: gradient at the current point, multiply by η (ηₜ if a schedule), subtract from each coordinate. Repeat.

flashcards.front: A step went far but f did not fall. What happened?
flashcards.back: The step overshot the valley (η too big). Judge a step by f, not by how far it moved.

quiz.q: In wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η∇f(wₜ), why is there a minus sign?
options: The gradient points uphill, so we go the other way
quiz.explain: The gradient points to steepest increase; the minimum is downhill.

quiz.q: The gradient is zero and the second derivative is negative. The point is…
quiz.explain: Negative second derivative means a maximum (slide 7).

quiz.q: The step size is far too large. What may happen?
quiz.explain: Slide 11: too large a step overshoots the target, fails to converge, or diverges.
Exponential decay is η₀·e^(−kt); inverse is η₀/(1 + kt).

blocks.text: How to recognise it

items: 'Perform two iterations of gradient descent', 'starting from', 'learning rate', 'step size', sometimes 'schedule'.
A simple function (a quadratic or a squared-error loss) and a starting point.

blocks.text: wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η∇f(wₜ)        ηₜ = η₀ / (1 + k·t)
Standard steps

items: Find the gradient: one partial derivative per variable.
Work out the step size (ηₜ if there is a schedule).
Put the current point into the gradient.
Subtract η × gradient from each coordinate.
Repeat, showing each line.
If asked for convexity, add the Hessian and Sylvester's criterion.

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: Judge progress by f, not by distance moved. Too large a step overshoots.
